meta.status: First 6 summaries drafted 2026-10-16 from the implementation brief; 13 more added 2026-11-08 so that every JEE technical area has one, drawn from sources already curated in solutions.json and link-checked that day. Source landing pages were checked for title, year and scope; the full documents were not re-read. Indicator links are candidate mappings against the exact JEE v3 wording, not claims that a practice raises a score.

sourceTypes.guideline: Normative WHO/partner guidance. Recommends what to do; it is not itself an effectiveness study.
sourceTypes.systematic-review: Peer-reviewed or WHO-commissioned review of published studies.
sourceTypes.tool: Operational tool, handbook or surveillance system.
sourceTypes.protocol: Technical protocol for surveillance or investigation.
sourceTypes.WHO benchmark: WHO benchmark actions for the technical area.
sourceTypes.peer-reviewed: Research article in a peer-reviewed journal.
sourceTypes.case-study: Description of what one country or organisation did; not evidence that it works elsewhere.
sourceTypes.conference abstract: Short meeting abstract; peer review is light and the full study may not be published.
sourceTypes.commentary: Opinion or comment piece in a journal; not original research.
sourceTypes.event page: Web page about an event or meeting.

practices.title: Multisectoral One Health coordination
practices.summary: Human, animal, food and environment sectors agree roles, share data and run joint surveillance, investigation and response, and test the arrangement in exercises and real events.
practices.mechanism: A standing mechanism with named responsibilities and agreed data-sharing lets signals from one sector trigger action in another, instead of relying on ad hoc contacts.
implementation: Formal coordination body with a written mandate and focal points in each sector
Agreed protocols for data sharing and joint risk assessment
Joint investigation and response procedures for priority zoonoses
Exercises and after-action reviews that feed back into the plan
practices.strength: Normative and widely endorsed. The sources set out a framework and tools; they do not report outcome data on JEE scores or outbreak results.
practices.context: Written for all countries; the operational tool for zoonoses was designed to help national authorities start joint work between sectors.
practices.limitations: Governance arrangements differ by country, so mechanisms cannot be copied as they are. A mechanism on paper does not show that it functions; exercises and real events are the test.

sources.citation: FAO, UNEP, WHO and WOAH. One health joint plan of action (2022-2026): working together for the health of humans, animals, plants and the environment. 2022.
FAO, OIE, WHO. Taking a multisectoral, One Health approach: a tripartite guide to addressing zoonotic diseases in countries. 2019.

practices.title: AMR surveillance linked to stewardship
practices.summary: Representative laboratory data on antimicrobial resistance and use is fed back to clinicians and public health programmes so that it changes prescribing and infection control, across human, animal and food sectors.
practices.mechanism: Surveillance only changes practice when results return to the sites that generate them and to the people who set policy.
implementation: Standardised data collection through a shared system (for example WHO GLASS)
Feedback of results to reporting laboratories and facilities
Stewardship activities in human health, plus data and action in animal health and agriculture
Links to the national action plan on AMR
practices.strength: GLASS is WHO's standardised system for AMR data; the Global Action Plan is the agreed policy framework. Neither is an effectiveness study.
practices.context: GLASS reports enrolment of more than 100 countries and territories and builds capacity to collect and share data, but the animal-health coverage is still being developed.
practices.limitations: Needs functioning laboratories and data systems first. Local implementation needs differ, and the sources do not show that enrolling in GLASS raises a JEE score.

sources.citation: WHO. Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS).
WHO. Global action plan on antimicrobial resistance. 2015.

practices.title: Laboratory quality and referral network
practices.summary: A tiered diagnostic network with validated specimen referral and transport, a quality management system, external quality assessment and documented biosafety risk assessment, with a loop for corrective action.
practices.mechanism: Reliable results depend on specimens reaching the right laboratory in good condition and on laboratories that detect and correct their own errors.
implementation: Map laboratory tiers and the referral routes between them
Quality management system with external quality assessment
Biosafety risk assessment and corrective-action tracking
Specimen transport arrangements tested in practice
practices.strength: Authoritative WHO guidance and handbooks. These describe accepted practice; they are not studies of outcomes.
practices.context: Written for laboratories at different levels of resource; the biosafety manual uses a risk-based approach.
practices.limitations: Quality systems take sustained funding and staff.

sources.citation: WHO. Laboratory quality management system: handbook. 2011.
WHO. Laboratory biosafety manual, 4th edition. 2020.

practices.title: Public health emergency operations centre readiness
practices.summary: Defined activation levels, incident management roles, interoperable situation reporting, rosters and logistics, tested through regular exercises with tracked corrective actions.
practices.mechanism: A centre that is activated, staffed and exercised on a routine basis can coordinate faster than one designed on paper and used first in a crisis.
implementation: Activation criteria and levels written into procedures
Incident management structure with trained, rostered staff
Situation reporting that other sectors can use
Discussion-based and functional exercises, followed by tracked corrective actions
practices.strength: WHO's 2013 systematic review is the main evidence source; its landing page does not state the number of studies or the findings, which were not read for this page. The handbook is operational guidance.
practices.context: The handbook is meant for countries building a centre; the review looks at how centres are described and run.
practices.limitations: The review is more than ten years old. Evidence on whether a centre improves outcomes is thin, so use these as sources of design options.

sources.citation: WHO. A systematic review of public health emergency operations centres (EOC). 2013.
WHO. Handbook for developing a public health emergency operations centre, part C.

practices.title: Emergency risk communication and community feedback
practices.summary: Trusted local partnerships set up before an emergency, two-way feedback, audience segmentation, accessible multilingual channels, and a way to change messages based on questions and rumours.
practices.mechanism: Messages reach and are acted on when they are shaped with the people they are for, and when the system listens as well as broadcasts.
implementation: Build relationships with community and civil society groups in advance
Collect and use community questions and rumours
Segment audiences and use accessible, multilingual channels
Integrate risk communication into preparedness and response structures and exercise it
practices.strength: The WHO guideline is normative. The systematic review behind it included 21 studies for integrating risk communication into the response and 24 for information sharing and coordination; the authors rated confidence in the synthesised findings as moderate.
practices.context: Evidence comes mostly from qualitative and case-based studies, with few from low- and middle-income countries.

sources.citation: WHO. Communicating risk in public health emergencies: a WHO guideline for emergency risk communication (ERC) policy and practice. 2018.

Jha A, Lin L, Short SM, Argentini G, Gamhewage G, Savoia E. Integrating emergency risk communication (ERC) into the public health system response: systematic review of literature to aid formulation of the 2017 WHO guideline for ERC policy and practice. PLoS One 2018;13(10):e0205555.

practices.title: Infection prevention and control programme with monitoring
practices.summary: A multimodal IPC programme with governance, guidance, training, supplies and infrastructure, and monitoring or audit with feedback, supported by surveillance of health care-associated infections that feeds improvement.
practices.mechanism: Programme components reinforce each other: guidance and training only stick when supplies exist and audit results are fed back to staff.
implementation: National IPC programme with a trained lead and a budget
Evidence-based guidance and training for health workers
Surveillance of health care-associated infections with feedback
Monitoring and audit of practice, and a safe, supplied facility environment
practices.strength: WHO describes its 2016 guideline as the first international evidence-based guidance on IPC core components, for the national and acute health care facility level. The 2022 global report describes status, not effectiveness.
practices.context: The guideline is described as applicable to any country with local adaptation; it covers national level and acute care facilities.
practices.limitations: The guideline covers acute care facilities, not all levels of care. The sources do not show that a programme raises a JEE score.

sources.citation: WHO. Guidelines on core components of infection prevention and control programmes at the national and acute health care facility level. 2016.
WHO. Global report on infection prevention and control. 2022.

practices.title: Legal mapping against IHR obligations
practices.summary: A structured review maps national laws against IHR obligations, records gaps and gives emergency functions such as declarations and the operations centre an explicit legal basis.
practices.mechanism: Emergency powers that are written down, tested and known to officials can be used quickly; gaps found in peacetime can be closed before a crisis forces improvised decisions.
implementation: Map existing laws and regulations against IHR obligations with a standard checklist
Agree which gaps need new law, regulation or administrative orders
Give the emergency operations centre and incident decisions a legal basis
Train legal staff and check the framework in exercises and after real events
practices.strength: Practical tools and normative guidance. They describe what a sound legal framework covers; none measures the effect of legal reform on response outcomes.
practices.context: Used in all regions; the WHO toolkit dates from 2009, the IFRC guidance and the RTSL checklist reflect COVID-19 experience.
practices.limitations: Legal systems differ, so templates need national adaptation. A law on paper says little about whether officials know and use it.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. International Health Regulations (2005) toolkit for implementation in national legislation. 2009.
International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. Guidance on law and public health emergency preparedness and response. 2021.
Resolve to Save Lives. Checklist and template for IHR legal analysis. 2025.
WHO Regional Office for Africa. PHEOC legal framework guide. 2021.

practices.title: Costed plans and fast emergency funds
practices.summary: Preparedness actions are costed and placed in regular budgets, and a contingency mechanism can release response money within days of an alert.
practices.mechanism: Costing turns a plan into budget lines that ministries of finance can fund; a pre-agreed release mechanism removes the delay between an alert and the first spending.
implementation: Cost the national action plan for health security activity by activity
Compare needs with allocated budgets and track disbursement, not only allocation
Set up a contingency fund or budget line with clear release rules
Know how to request external emergency funds such as WHO's Contingency Fund
practices.strength: Assessment and costing tools plus strategy documents. They describe financing arrangements; outcome evidence on response speed is mostly descriptive.
practices.context: Developed by WHO, the World Bank and Resolve to Save Lives for low- and middle-income countries, but the logic applies everywhere.
practices.limitations: Budget processes and fiscal space vary widely. A costed plan does not guarantee money, and emergency funds can be slow if release rules are unclear.

sources.citation: World Bank. Health Security Financing Assessment Tool (HSFAT). 2018.
World Health Organization. Delivering global health security through sustainable financing. 2018.
Resolve to Save Lives. Action-based costing for national action plans for health security.
World Health Organization. NAPHS for all: a country implementation guide for national action plans for health security. 2019.

practices.title: A National IHR Focal Point that works around the clock
practices.summary: The National IHR Focal Point has a clear mandate, staff reachable 24/7, standard procedures for assessing and notifying events, and links to every sector that may detect one.
practices.mechanism: A reachable, mandated focal point with tested procedures shortens the time from detection to notification and to coordinated action across sectors.
implementation: Formal mandate and placement of the focal point, with named staff and back-up
24/7 contact that is tested regularly
Standard operating procedures using the IHR Annex 2 decision instrument
Contacts in animal health, food safety, chemical, radiation and points of entry, checked in exercises
practices.strength: Normative WHO and PAHO guidance plus training material. Describes good arrangements; evidence of impact comes mainly from after-action reviews.
practices.context: Applies to all States Parties; PAHO's operational framework and workshop toolkit come from the Americas.
practices.limitations: Focal point placement and powers differ by country. Regular staff turnover means procedures and contacts need constant upkeep.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. National IHR Focal Points, including the National IHR Focal Point Guide.
Pan American Health Organization. Overview of IHR National Focal Point functions: operational framework. 2023.
World Health Organization. WHO guidance for the use of Annex 2 of the International Health Regulations (2005). 2010.
World Health Organization. WHO simulation exercise manual. 2017.

practices.title: Foodborne event detection and a food safety emergency plan
practices.summary: Indicator- and event-based surveillance picks up foodborne events, a national plan sets thresholds, roles and recall procedures, and INFOSAN contacts share information across borders.
practices.mechanism: Linking surveillance, food control and international notification means a contaminated product can be traced and withdrawn before more people are exposed.
implementation: Event- and indicator-based surveillance for priority foodborne diseases
National food safety emergency response plan with thresholds and named roles
INFOSAN emergency contact point and a national information-sharing protocol
Trained outbreak investigation teams and risk communication procedures
practices.strength: FAO/WHO frameworks and templates, plus one Codex country case study. Guidance-based; outcome data are limited to case descriptions.
practices.context: Global FAO/WHO guidance; the Honduras case shows a 2021 Salmonella outbreak handled with Codex standards.
practices.limitations: Food control is often split across ministries, which the plan must reconcile. Guidance from 2008–2010 predates whole-genome sequencing in outbreak work.

sources.citation: FAO and WHO. FAO/WHO framework for developing national food safety emergency response plans. 2010.
World Health Organization. Using indicator- and event-based surveillance to detect foodborne events (stage one booklet). 2017.
WHO and FAO. INFOSAN members guide, web annex: template national protocol for information sharing during food safety events. 2020.
Codex Alimentarius Commission (FAO/WHO). Codex case study: Honduras, 2021 Salmonella Braenderup outbreak linked to melons.

practices.title: National biosafety and biosecurity oversight
practices.summary: A national inventory shows which facilities hold dangerous pathogens, a risk-based regulatory framework licenses and inspects them, and staff are trained in biosafety and biosecurity.
practices.mechanism: Knowing where dangerous agents are, and holding facilities to risk-based rules, reduces the chance of accidental release or misuse and lets collections be consolidated.
implementation: National inventory of facilities holding dangerous pathogens, kept up to date
Risk-based regulation with licensing, inspection and incident reporting
Biosecurity audits with a standard checklist or self-assessment tool
Training and competence requirements aligned with the WHO manual or ISO 35001
practices.strength: WHO normative guidance plus peer-reviewed methods and tools (inventory method, biosecurity checklist, vulnerability scan) and a Kenyan baseline survey. Methods are tested in practice; impact on incident rates is not measured.
practices.context: The inventory method and checklists were developed with the Dutch Biosecurity Office; the Kenyan survey shows a baseline before legislation.
practices.limitations: Regulation needs inspection capacity to mean anything. Biosecurity information is sensitive, which limits what can be published or shared.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. Laboratory biosafety manual, 4th edition. 2020.
World Health Organization. Laboratory biosecurity guidance. 2024.
Vennis IM, Bleijs DA, Brizee S, et al. Systematic approach towards establishing a National Inventory of Dangerous Pathogens. Glob Health Action. 2021;14(1):1971866.
Ndhine EO, Slotved HC, Osoro EM, et al. A biosecurity survey in Kenya, November 2014 to February 2015. Health Secur. 2016;14(4):205-213.

practices.title: Reaching under-vaccinated groups and readiness for mass campaigns
practices.summary: Programmes find out who is missed and why, verify coverage data, keep the cold chain in shape, and have a plan for outbreak vaccination with safety monitoring.
practices.mechanism: Targeting the reasons behind low uptake closes immunity gaps that fuel outbreaks; a managed supply chain and AEFI surveillance make rapid campaigns possible and keep trust.
implementation: Behavioural and social drivers surveys to find why groups are missed
Tailored interventions for those groups (TIP approach)
Data quality review and Effective Vaccine Management assessment
Outbreak vaccination plan with AEFI surveillance and investigation
practices.strength: WHO tools and strategy, widely used in national programmes. The TIP and BeSD approaches are evaluated in several countries, but outcome evidence varies by setting.
practices.context: Global tools; TIP comes from the WHO European Region and is used in high- and middle-income countries.
practices.limitations: Hesitancy and access barriers are local and change over time. Coverage data can look good while pockets of low coverage remain.

sources.citation: WHO Regional Office for Europe. TIP: tailoring immunization programmes. 2019.
World Health Organization. Behavioural and social drivers of vaccination: tools and practical guidance for achieving high uptake. 2022.
World Health Organization. Global manual on surveillance of adverse events following immunization. 2016.
World Health Organization. Immunization Agenda 2030: a global strategy to leave no one behind. 2020.

practices.title: Early warning with a timeliness target (7-1-7)
practices.summary: Indicator- and event-based surveillance feed one alert system, every signal is verified, and each event is timed against 7 days to detect, 1 to notify and 7 to respond, with bottlenecks reviewed.
practices.mechanism: A simple timeliness target makes delays visible after every event and turns them into specific fixes, rather than general calls to strengthen surveillance.
implementation: Event-based surveillance alongside routine indicator-based reporting
Alert logbook with verification and rapid risk assessment
7-1-7 timing recorded for every event, with bottlenecks and fixes
Regular analysis and sharing of surveillance data across levels and sectors
practices.strength: WHO operational guides plus a Lancet Global Health commentary on 7-1-7. Early country reports show bottlenecks being found and fixed; controlled outcome studies are lacking.
practices.context: IDSR is the African standard; 7-1-7 is used by a growing group of countries with Resolve to Save Lives and WHO.
practices.limitations: Timeliness says nothing about events that are never detected. Measuring 7-1-7 needs reliable dates for onset, detection and response.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. Early warning, alert and response (EWAR) in emergencies: an operational guide. 2023.
WHO Regional Office for Africa. Technical guidelines for integrated disease surveillance and response in the African Region, 3rd edition. 2019.
Resolve to Save Lives. Implementation of the 7-1-7 target for detection, notification and response.
Mayigane LN, Vedrasco L, Chungong S. 7-1-7: the promise of tangible results through agility and accountability. Lancet Glob Health. 2023.

practices.title: Workforce strategy, field epidemiology and surge
practices.summary: A workforce strategy based on public health competencies, accredited field epidemiology training, and a roster that can surge staff into a response.
practices.mechanism: Competency frameworks and accredited training produce people who can investigate and lead; a pre-agreed surge roster means they can be deployed without improvisation.
implementation: Workforce strategy based on the essential public health functions competency framework
Field epidemiology training at frontline, intermediate and advanced levels, with accreditation
Surge roster and deployment procedures linked to the Global Health Emergency Corps
Workforce data (national accounts) and staff self-assessment of emergency competencies
practices.strength: WHO frameworks, TEPHINET accreditation standards and a peer-reviewed self-assessment tool from the European Union. Good practice is well described; workforce outcome data are thin.
practices.context: Global frameworks; the self-assessment tool was developed for European public health institutes.
practices.limitations: Trained staff leave when career paths are weak. Surge arrangements need funding and legal cover to work across institutions.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. Global competency and outcomes framework for the essential public health functions. 2024.
World Health Organization. Global health emergency corps framework. 2024.
TEPHINET. FETP accreditation and quality improvement.
Hayes JS, Barreto M, Kalin-Manttari L, et al. Development of a workforce self-assessment tool for public health emergency preparedness. Eur J Public Health. 2024.

practices.title: Joint public health and security investigations
practices.summary: Public health, law enforcement, customs and the military agree in advance how they share information, investigate together and support each other in a suspected deliberate or major biological event.
practices.mechanism: Prior agreements and joint training let both sides act on the same event without blocking each other: evidence is preserved while the outbreak response goes ahead.
implementation: Memorandum of understanding between health and security authorities
Joint investigation procedures and information-sharing rules
Joint training and exercises, for example with INTERPOL or national police academies
Civil-military collaboration framework for logistics and surge support
practices.strength: Handbooks and frameworks from the FBI, INTERPOL and WHO. Based on experience and exercises; there is little published outcome evidence.
practices.context: The joint investigations handbook was written with international partners; WHO's civil-military framework covers all hazards.
practices.limitations: Security information is often classified, which limits sharing. Arrangements must respect human rights and the separate mandates of each sector.

sources.citation: FBI and partners. Joint criminal and epidemiological investigations handbook, international edition. 2016.
World Health Organization. National civil-military collaboration framework for strengthening health emergency preparedness. 2021.
INTERPOL. Bioterrorism capacity building and training.
World Health Organization. Multisectoral preparedness coordination framework: best practices, case studies and key elements. 2020.

practices.title: Continuity of essential health services in emergencies
practices.summary: Countries define which services must continue, facilities have tested continuity plans, and rapid surveys track disruptions so services can be restored quickly.
practices.mechanism: Planning which services to protect, and monitoring disruptions as they happen, prevents the indirect deaths that follow when routine care stops during an emergency.
implementation: National list of essential services to maintain in emergencies
Facility continuity plans, tested and reviewed
Rapid surveys of service disruption and recovery
Hospital emergency response checklist for surge and referral
practices.strength: WHO operational guidance shaped by COVID-19, plus a peer-reviewed analysis of rapid key-informant surveys. Monitoring methods are tested; the effect of continuity plans is less well measured.
practices.context: Developed during COVID-19 but written for all hazards; the surveys covered many WHO Member States.
practices.limitations: Continuity depends on staff and supplies that emergencies strain. Survey data rely on key informants and may miss local disruption.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. Health service continuity planning for public health emergencies: a handbook for health facilities. 2021.
World Health Organization. Maintaining essential health services: operational guidance for the COVID-19 context. 2020.

Rivas-Morello B, Horemans D, Viswanathan K, et al. Assessing capacities and resilience of health services during the COVID-19 pandemic: lessons from rapid key informant surveys. Front Public Health. 2023.
WHO Regional Office for Europe. Hospital emergency response checklist. 2011.

practices.title: Points of entry linked to national surveillance and contingency plans
practices.summary: Designated airports, ports and ground crossings meet routine core capacities, have tested contingency plans, feed national surveillance and agree cross-border arrangements with neighbours.
practices.mechanism: Plans and procedures agreed in advance let a point of entry handle an ill traveller or conveyance quickly and proportionately, without improvised border measures.
implementation: Assessment of routine core capacities at designated points of entry
Public health emergency contingency plan per point of entry, tested in exercises
Reporting from points of entry into national surveillance
Cross-border agreements at ground crossings and a risk-based approach to travel measures
practices.strength: WHO assessment tools, handbooks and technical considerations. Normative; evaluations of travel measures during COVID-19 were mixed.
practices.context: Global WHO guidance; the ground crossings handbook focuses on land borders and neighbouring countries.
practices.limitations: Many points of entry are informal and outside these systems. Travel measures can be costly and of limited effect if not risk-based.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. IHR (2005): a guide for public health emergency contingency planning at designated points of entry. 2012.
World Health Organization. IHR (2005): assessment tool for core capacity requirements at designated airports, ports and ground crossings. 2009.
World Health Organization. Handbook for public health capacity-building at ground crossings and cross-border collaboration. 2020.
World Health Organization. Coordinated public health surveillance between points of entry and national health surveillance systems. 2014.

practices.title: Chemical incident preparedness with poison centres and site plans
practices.summary: Health authorities, poison centres and industry share surveillance and planning: hazardous sites are registered and have off-site plans, and chemical events are assessed and notified under the IHR.
practices.mechanism: Knowing where hazardous chemicals are and who does what lets responders act within hours; poison centres provide expertise and early signals of exposure.
implementation: Register of hazardous installations with safety reports and off-site emergency plans
Poison centre linked to surveillance and IHR notification
Investigation procedures for illnesses of possible chemical origin
Local preparedness that brings operators, authorities and residents together (APELL)
practices.strength: WHO manuals, OECD guiding principles and the EU Seveso regime as a legal model. Long experience in industrial safety; health outcome evidence is mostly from case reviews.
practices.context: Seveso III shows how one region regulates major-accident hazards; the WHO and OECD texts are global.
practices.limitations: Responsibility is split between environment, labour, industry and health ministries. Small and illegal sites often fall outside registers.

sources.citation: World Health Organization. WHO manual for the public health management of chemical incidents. 2009.
World Health Organization. Guidelines for establishing a poison centre. 2020.
OECD. OECD Guiding Principles for Chemical Accident Prevention, Preparedness and Response, third edition. 2023.
European Environment Agency. Seveso III Directive (2012/18/EU): Seveso establishments, industrial reporting portal.

practices.title: Radiation emergency arrangements and medical response
practices.summary: Arrangements follow IAEA requirements, hospitals have ready procedures for triage, decontamination and follow-up of exposed people, stockpiles are managed, and international networks can be called on.
practices.mechanism: A pre-agreed protection strategy and medical procedures allow a response sized to the event, avoiding both under-reaction and harmful over-reaction such as unnecessary evacuation.
implementation: National arrangements meeting IAEA GSR Part 7, with a protection strategy
Hospital and first-responder procedures for triage, decontamination and registration
Stockpile policy for radiological and nuclear emergencies
Access to REMPAN, BioDoseNet and the IAEA Incident and Emergency Centre
practices.strength: IAEA safety requirements and WHO policy advice, built on experience from past accidents. Strong consensus; outcome evidence comes from case reviews of real events.
practices.context: Applies to all countries, whether or not they have nuclear facilities; many hazards come from radioactive sources in medicine and industry.
practices.limitations: Rare events make it hard to keep skills current without exercises. Responsibilities are shared with radiation regulators outside health.

sources.citation: IAEA and co-sponsors. Preparedness and response for a nuclear or radiological emergency (IAEA GSR Part 7). 2015.
International Atomic Energy Agency. Generic procedures for medical response during a nuclear or radiological emergency (EPR-Medical 2024). 2024.
World Health Organization. National stockpiles for radiological and nuclear emergencies: policy advice. 2023.
World Health Organization. Radiation Emergency Medical Preparedness and Assistance Network (REMPAN).
